passages.t: The Beatitudes: who is well off in God's kingdom
passages.happening:
Crowds have gathered from all over the region (4:25). Jesus goes up on the mountain and sits down, and his disciples come to him. Then he begins to teach.

He starts with eight sayings that all begin the same way: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (verse 3). Then those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those who are persecuted for doing right. A ninth saying turns to the listeners directly: ‘Blessed are you’ when people insult and persecute you because of me (verse 11).

These sayings are called the Beatitudes, from the Latin word for ‘blessed’.
passages.hearers:
Teachers in Jesus' world sat down to teach (Luke 4:20). When Jesus sits on the mountain, his hearers know a lesson is starting. Readers who know Israel's story may also think of Moses, who went up a mountain and brought God's law down to the people. Matthew never says Jesus is a new Moses, but many scholars think he arranges the scene so the comparison is hard to miss.

A saying that begins ‘Blessed is’ was familiar. The book of Psalms opens with one: “Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked” (Psalm 1:1). Such a saying is not a wish. It is a statement about someone's condition before God. It means something like ‘how well off they are’, or ‘God's favor is on them’.

What would surprise a hearer is who Jesus names. Not the rich, the strong or the respected. The poor in spirit are people who know they have nothing to bring God. Those who mourn may grieve their own sin, the state of God's people, or a loss of their own. The meek are not weak. They are people who do not grab power for themselves and leave their cause with God.

The list falls into two halves. The first four are about need: poverty, grief, lowliness, hunger. The next four are about how people live: mercy, a clean heart, making peace, standing firm when it costs. The first and the eighth end with the same promise, ‘theirs is the kingdom of heaven’, which wraps the whole list in one gift.
passages.ot:
Are the Beatitudes a list of things we must achieve to get into the kingdom, or good news for people who have nothing? Readers have taken them both ways. Some stress that they describe the character of Jesus' followers, a way of life to grow into. Others stress that they are announcements of grace, spoken first to the poor and the grieving who could earn nothing. Many hold both: God's gift comes first, and it makes people merciful, pure and peaceable.

The last saying is about persecution. It is not a call to seek suffering, or to treat every hard word as persecution. It is a promise to those who suffer because they belong to Jesus, that they stand with the prophets and their reward is with God.
passages.hard: Read the list slowly and ask which of these people you would naturally call fortunate. Jesus begins his greatest teaching with the poor, the grieving and the hungry. Where do you feel empty or sad before God? These words say that is not a place God has left. It may be where his kingdom begins.
passages.asks: Several of the sayings echo the Old Testament. Isaiah 61 speaks of one anointed by the Spirit “to preach good news to the poor” and “to comfort all who mourn” (Isaiah 61:1-2). Psalm 37:11 says “the meek will inherit the land.” Jesus widens the land to ‘the earth’. Seeing God (verse 8) recalls Psalm 24, where only those with clean hands and a pure heart may go up to God's holy hill.

passages.happening:
Jesus turns from ‘they’ to ‘you’. “You are the salt of the earth” (verse 13). If salt loses its taste, it is good for nothing but to be thrown out and walked on.

“You are the light of the world. A city on a hill cannot be hidden” (verse 14). No one lights a lamp and puts it under a basket. They set it on a stand so it lights the whole house. In the same way, Jesus says, let your light shine before people, so that they see your good deeds and give glory to your Father in heaven (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Salt was one of the most ordinary things in an ancient kitchen. It flavored food and kept meat and fish from going bad. In Israel's worship every grain offering was seasoned with salt (Leviticus 2:13). How salt could lose its taste has been explained in different ways, and no one explanation is agreed. The picture is plain enough: salt that does not do what salt does is useless.

The lamp was a small clay oil lamp. Set on a stand, Jesus says, “it gives light to everyone in the house.” The ‘basket’ was a container for measuring grain. Putting it over a lamp would be pointless.

Notice who Jesus is speaking to. Not the powerful or the educated. Fishermen, farmers and the crowds who have just heard that the poor and the meek are well off. These are the people he calls the salt of the earth and the light of the world.
passages.ot: Verse 16 says to let people see your good deeds. But in the next chapter Jesus says, “Be careful not to perform your righteous acts before men to be seen by them” (6:1). Is that a contradiction? The difference is the goal. Here the deeds are seen so that people ‘glorify your Father in heaven’. In chapter 6 the deeds are done so that people will praise the one doing them. The question in both places is who gets the glory.
passages.hard: Salt and light do their work by being different from what is around them, and by being close to it. Salt kept in the jar preserves nothing. Ask where your faith has been kept in the jar. And ask whether the good you do points people to yourself, or to the Father.
passages.asks: Israel had long been meant to be a light. God says to his servant in Isaiah, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Isaiah also pictures God's mountain raised above the hills, with “all nations” streaming to it to learn God's ways (Isaiah 2:2-3). A city on a hill that cannot be hidden would bring those pictures to mind.

passages.t: Not to abolish, but to fulfill
passages.happening:
Jesus says plainly what he has come to do. “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them” (verse 17). Not the smallest letter or stroke of the Law will pass away until everything is accomplished. Whoever breaks the least command and teaches others to do so will be least in the kingdom. Whoever keeps and teaches them will be great.

Then comes a startling line: unless your righteousness goes beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
‘The Law and the Prophets’ was a common way of naming Israel's Scriptures. Jesus is a Jewish teacher speaking to Jews about their own holy books. He is not setting himself against them.

The ‘jot’ and ‘stroke of a pen’ are the smallest letter of the alphabet and the smallest mark a scribe could make. Jesus is saying that God's word is not careless in any part.

Scribes were the trained experts who taught and applied the Law. The Pharisees were a movement of devout Jews, admired by ordinary people for their care to keep it. So verse 20 would have shocked the crowd. If even these people were not righteous enough, who could be? The rest of the chapter answers. The righteousness Jesus means goes deeper, to the heart, where anger, desire and hatred begin.

‘Fulfill’ means to fill full, to bring something to its goal. Matthew has already used the word again and again for how Jesus' life completes what the Scriptures promised (1:22; 2:15; 4:14).
passages.ot: If Jesus did not come to abolish the Law, why do most Christians not keep all of it, such as the food laws and the sacrifices? Christians have given more than one answer. Many have divided the Law into moral, ceremonial and civil parts, and held that the moral law still binds, while the sacrifices and the laws for Israel as a nation found their goal in Christ. Others prefer to say that the whole Law is fulfilled in Christ and is now read through him and through love, which Paul calls “the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:10). Mark notes that Jesus' teaching meant “all foods are clean” (Mark 7:19), and the early church decided that Gentile believers need not keep the whole Law of Moses (Acts 15:19-20). What all these readings share is verse 17 itself. Jesus does not treat Israel's Scriptures as a mistake to be thrown away. He treats them as God's word, brought to its goal.
passages.hard: Jesus asks for more than rule-keeping, not less. That is good news and hard news. It means God cares about who you are when no one is checking. Where have you been content with the outward line, and what might it mean to let God's word reach the place it is aimed at?
passages.asks: The prophets had looked forward to a day when God's law would be written on the heart. “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). Ezekiel spoke of a new heart and God's Spirit within (Ezekiel 36:26-27). Jesus' teaching in the verses that follow aims at exactly that place: the heart.

passages.happening:
Now come six sayings that each begin, ‘You have heard that it was said’, and continue, ‘But I tell you’.

The first is about murder. The Law says, “Do not murder.” Jesus says that anyone who is angry with his brother will face judgment, and anyone who insults him faces worse (verse 22).

Then two pictures. If you are at the altar with your gift and remember that your brother has something against you, leave the gift, go and make peace, then come back and offer it. And settle with your opponent quickly, on the way to court, before the judge hands you over and you are thrown into prison.
passages.hearers:
‘Raca’ is an Aramaic insult meaning something like ‘empty-head’ or ‘good for nothing’. It appears nowhere else in the Bible. The Sanhedrin was the highest Jewish council. ‘The fire of hell’ is literally ‘the Gehenna of fire’. Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, where in Judah's worst days children had been burned as sacrifices (Jeremiah 7:31). Its name became a word for God's final judgment. You may hear that it was a burning rubbish dump, but there is no ancient evidence for that.

The altar picture would land hard. Bringing a gift to the altar was holy work, done in the temple in Jerusalem. Jesus says that making peace with your brother comes first. Later Jewish teachers said something close. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, teaches that the Day of Atonement wins forgiveness for sins against God, but not for wrongs done to a neighbor until the neighbor has been made peace with (Yoma 8:9).

The ‘you have heard ... but I tell you’ pattern is not Jesus attacking the Law. In this first case he quotes one of the Ten Commandments and goes to its root. Murder begins in contempt. A person who never despises his brother will never kill him.
passages.ot:
Is all anger sin? The New Testament does not say so. Jesus himself looked at people “with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart” (Mark 3:5). Paul writes, “Be angry, yet do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). Anger at real wrong can be right. What Jesus warns against is the anger that holds a grudge, despises a person, and wants them gone.

Nor does ‘go and be reconciled’ mean a person who has been harmed must go back to someone dangerous. Making peace takes two. Paul says, “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18). Sometimes the safest and most honest step is distance, and help from others.
passages.hard: Is there someone who has something against you? Jesus says that matters to God more than your gift. Think of one step you could take this week, a call, an apology, a debt paid. And notice how you speak of people in your head. Contempt is where the road to murder starts.
passages.asks: The command is from the Ten Commandments: “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). The Law already reached past the act. “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart” (Leviticus 19:17).

passages.t: Desire, and the eye and the hand
passages.happening:
The second saying is about adultery. The Law says, “Do not commit adultery.” Jesus says that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (verse 28).

Then he uses the strongest pictures in the sermon. If your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away. If your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell.
passages.hearers:
The words ‘to lust after her’ point to a look with a purpose: looking in order to want and to take, at least in the mind. Jesus is not speaking about noticing that someone is beautiful. He is speaking about desire that treats a person as something to have.

Notice who carries the blame. Jesus puts the responsibility on the man who looks. He does not tell women to hide. He tells men to guard their own hearts.

Jesus names an eye and a hand, parts no one would want to lose. His point is that nothing is too precious to give up if it is leading you into sin.
passages.ot:
Does Jesus want people to cut off their hands or put out their eyes? No. He is using a strong picture, as teachers in his culture often did, to show how serious sin is. The point is to cut off whatever leads you into sin, a habit, a place, a relationship, a screen, however much it costs. The church has always taught that this is not a command to harm the body. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone now: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line.

Some readers also worry that every passing thought makes them guilty of adultery. Jesus is naming where sin starts, so that it can be stopped there. He is not saying that temptation itself is sin. Jesus was tempted too (4:1).
passages.hard: What feeds the wrong kind of desire in your life? Jesus does not ask you to harm your body. He asks you to be honest about what you keep looking at, and to be willing to give it up. What would that cost you, and is it worth more than your heart?
passages.asks: The command is from the Ten Commandments: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14). The last commandment already went to the heart, forbidding a person to covet a neighbor's wife (Exodus 20:17).

passages.happening:
The third saying is about divorce. Moses' law allowed a man to end his marriage in writing: “Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce” (verse 31). Jesus says that anyone who divorces his wife, “except for sexual immorality,” brings adultery upon her, and anyone who marries a divorced woman commits adultery (verse 32).

Jesus speaks about divorce again, at more length, in chapter 19.
passages.hearers:
The law in Deuteronomy 24:1 lets a man divorce his wife if he finds ‘some indecency’ in her, by writing her a certificate. What did ‘some indecency’ mean? The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, records the later memory of the debate (Gittin 9:10). The school of Shammai said a man could divorce only for something shameful, such as unfaithfulness. The school of Hillel said he could divorce even if she spoiled his dinner.

In Jewish law at that time only the husband could end a marriage. The certificate protected the woman, because it proved she was free to marry again. A woman sent away might have little way to live unless she married again. Many readers think that is why Jesus says the husband ‘brings adultery upon her’. Jesus puts the weight of what follows on the man who sends her away, not on her.
passages.ot:
Only Matthew has the words ‘except for sexual immorality’ (here and in 19:9). Mark, Luke and Paul give Jesus' teaching without them. Christians read the exception and the whole teaching in different ways, and each answer is held by careful readers. The Catholic Church teaches that a true sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved while both spouses live, though it allows separation and can declare that a true marriage never existed. Some Catholic scholars read the Greek word here as a marriage the law forbade, such as to a close relative. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be for life but, as an act of mercy, allow a second marriage with a service of repentance. Most Protestant churches read the exception, with Paul's words about a spouse who leaves (1 Corinthians 7:15), as showing that unfaithfulness and desertion can free the innocent partner to remarry. Many also count abuse as breaking the marriage covenant. Some read the exception as unfaithfulness during betrothal, as when Joseph planned to divorce Mary (1:19). These notes do not decide between them.

What all of them share is Jesus' main point. God meant marriage to last for life, and Jesus defends the one who is sent away.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.
passages.hard: Jesus moves the question from ‘How do I end this properly?’ to ‘What did God intend, and who gets hurt?’ If divorce has touched your life, by your choice or not, remember that these words were spoken to protect the one with no power. They are not a stone to throw at anyone, including yourself.
passages.asks: Jesus goes back behind the certificate to God's first purpose for marriage: “they will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). In chapter 19 he says, “Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart; but it was not this way from the beginning” (19:8).

passages.t: Oaths: let your yes be yes
passages.happening:
The fourth saying is about oaths. The ancients were told, ‘Do not break your oath, but fulfill your vows to the Lord.’ Jesus says, “But I tell you not to swear at all” (verse 34). Not by heaven, which is God's throne. Not by the earth, his footstool. Not by Jerusalem, the city of the great King. Not even by your own head, since you cannot make one hair white or black.

“Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’ Anything more comes from the evil one” (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
An oath called on God, or on something holy, as a witness that you were telling the truth. People swore by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem or by their own heads, and some argued about which oaths really counted. Jesus mocks that game in chapter 23: they said swearing by the temple meant nothing, but swearing by the gold of the temple was binding (23:16).

The problem was two levels of truth. Careful when you swore, careless when you did not. Jesus does away with the second level. A follower of his should be so honest that a plain yes is enough.

Jesus was not the only Jewish voice to say this. The historian Josephus says the Essenes, a strict Jewish group of the time, avoided swearing. They thought it worse than lying, because a person who cannot be believed without calling on God is already condemned (Jewish War 2.135).
passages.ot: May a Christian take an oath, for example in a court of law? Christians disagree. The Anabaptists of the 1500s read verse 34 plainly and refused all oaths, and some Christians still refuse them. Most churches have held that Jesus forbids careless and dishonest swearing, not a solemn oath when the law asks for one. They point out that Paul calls on God as his witness (2 Corinthians 1:23), and that God himself “guaranteed it with an oath” (Hebrews 6:17). James repeats Jesus' words (James 5:12). Whichever view a reader holds, the heart of the teaching is shared: plain, reliable truth in every word.
passages.hard: Do people need you to promise before they believe you? Think about where you shade the truth because ‘it doesn't really count’. Jesus asks for a life where every word counts.
passages.asks: The Law forbade swearing falsely by God's name (Leviticus 19:12) and told Israel to keep every vow: a man “must not break his word; he must do everything he has promised” (Numbers 30:2). It even said that if you do not make a vow, “you will not be guilty of sin” (Deuteronomy 23:22). Heaven as God's throne and the earth as his footstool is the language of Isaiah 66:1.

passages.happening: The fifth saying begins with an old rule of justice: “Eye for eye and tooth for tooth” (verse 38). Jesus says, ‘Do not resist an evil person.’ If someone slaps you on the right cheek, turn the other to him also. If someone wants to sue you for your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. If someone forces you to go one mile, go two. Give to the one who asks, and do not turn away the one who wants to borrow.
passages.hearers:
‘Eye for eye’ was a rule for judges, not permission for private revenge. It set a limit: the penalty must fit the harm and go no further. Its setting in Deuteronomy is a court, where “the judges shall investigate thoroughly” (Deuteronomy 19:18).

A slap on the right cheek is an insult as much as an injury. Many readers note that a right-handed person would strike the right cheek with the back of the hand. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, sets a heavier fine for a slap with the back of the hand than for an ordinary slap (Bava Kamma 8:6). The insult was the point.

The tunic was the garment worn next to the skin; the cloak was the outer one, which a poor man also slept in. The Law said a cloak taken as a pledge had to be given back by sunset (Exodus 22:26-27).

The word for ‘forces you to go’ is a borrowed word from Persian. It first meant the right of royal messengers to press people and animals into service. Matthew uses the same word when the soldiers force Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus' cross (27:32). Jesus' hearers knew what it was to be made to carry a stranger's load.
passages.ot:
Christians have read ‘do not resist an evil person’ in three main ways. Pacifists, such as the Anabaptists and their heirs the Mennonites, read it as forbidding all violence, and the novelist Leo Tolstoy (What I Believe, 1884) called it the key to the whole sermon. Martin Luther taught two kinds of duty: in your own cause, bear wrong without revenge, but a ruler or judge must protect others and punish wrong (Romans 13:4). The just war tradition, from Augustine to Thomas Aquinas, holds that love of neighbor can require lawful force to protect the innocent, within strict limits. These notes do not decide between them.

One thing must be said plainly. ‘Turn the other cheek’ is not a command to stay with someone who is hurting you. Jesus speaks of refusing revenge, not of accepting abuse. When an officer struck him, Jesus asked, “why did you strike Me?” (John 18:23). Paul used his rights under Roman law to stop a flogging (Acts 22:25). Seeking safety, and the protection of the law, is not disobedience to Jesus. If you are being harmed, tell someone you trust and get help.
passages.hard: Jesus asks his followers to break the cycle of getting even. Where do you keep score? Think of one person who has insulted or used you, and ask what refusing revenge would look like, while still keeping yourself and others safe.
passages.asks: The rule ‘eye for eye, tooth for tooth’ is found three times in the Law, in Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20 and Deuteronomy 19:21. The Old Testament also says, “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat” (Proverbs 25:21).

passages.happening:
The sixth saying: ‘You have heard that it was said, Love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ Jesus says, “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (verse 44). That is how you show you are children of your Father, who makes his sun rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the just and the unjust.

If you love only those who love you, what reward is that? Even tax collectors do that. If you greet only your own people, even Gentiles do that. “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (verse 48).
passages.hearers:
‘Love your neighbor’ is from the Law (Leviticus 19:18). ‘Hate your enemy’ is not found anywhere in the Old Testament. Jesus seems to be quoting the way some people summed up the Law, not the Law itself. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Community Rule told members to love the ‘sons of light’ and hate the ‘sons of darkness’, those outside their group. Some scholars think Jesus may have had teaching like that in mind. No one knows for certain.

Tax collectors were Jews who collected tolls for the rulers and were despised as cheats who worked with the powers in charge. Gentiles were non-Jews. Greeting only your own people, Jesus says, is nothing special.

‘Perfect’ translates a Greek word that means whole or complete, grown to its goal. In Luke's version of the saying Jesus says, “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36). The perfection in view is the Father's whole-hearted love, which does not stop at the edge of the people who love him back.
passages.ot:
‘Be perfect’ can sound like a demand no one can meet. Some readers take it as a goal to grow toward all life long. Some take it as the point where the sermon shows us our need of God's mercy. Others stress that ‘perfect’ here means complete in love, loving enemies as well as friends, not flawless in every way. Many hold more than one of these at once.

Loving an enemy does not mean pretending they did no wrong, or trusting someone who is still dangerous. It means wanting their good, praying for them, and refusing to wish them harm.
passages.hard: Who is your enemy? Name one person. Jesus asks you to pray for them, by name, this week. Not to excuse them, but to treat them the way the Father treats the world, with sun and rain they did not earn. Notice what that prayer does to you.
passages.asks: The Law already pushed past hatred. It told Israel to return an enemy's stray ox or donkey and to help an enemy's donkey that had fallen under its load (Exodus 23:4-5). Verse 48 echoes Leviticus 19:2, “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy,” and Deuteronomy 18:13, “You must be blameless before the LORD your God.”
